newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan rivals claim victories in east of country.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rivals claim victories in east of country.

text.p: The beleaguered Afghan government and the rebel Taleban militia claimed victories against each other on Thursday in fresh fighting after the rebels seized the main eastern town of Jalalabad on Wednesday.
Both sides reported heavy fighting in some districts of Nangarhar province, of which Jalalabad is the capital, and the adjoining Logar province.

President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government in Kabul said its forces had recaptured the strategic Hisarak district in the west of the eastern province of Nangarhar and Azra district in the adjoining Logar province, cutting off the Taleban supply route to Jalalabad from southern Afghanistan.
Taleban sources in neighbouring Pakistan said their Islamic militia had advanced north of Jalalabad early on Thursday and captured Behsud district.
There was no independent confirmation of either report.
A spokesman for Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar said in Kabul the government troops captured Hisarak on Thursday morning in an attack from Tizin and Jagdalak areas in Kabul province.
The government troops also captured Azra district in Logar, southwest of Hisarak, but high ground overlooking Azra bazaar was still held by Taleban, he said.
Taleban had taken Azra and Hisarak earlier this week to pave the way for their assault on Jalalabad.
A Taleban source, quoted by a Pakistan-based news service, said government jets had heavily bombed Azra town and its environs but there was no report of any ground attack there.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) also quoted a Taleban spokesman as saying that the militia fighters had forced government troops to withdraw from Darunta base northwest of Jalalabad after capturing Behsud district.
Hekmatyar's spokesman, Hamid Ibrahimi, acknowledged that Taleban captured the government mountain base of Shamshad in Nangarhar near the Pakistan border on Wednesday night.

The Taleban, which controls more than half of Afghanistan and seeks to topple Rabbani, seized most of Nangarhar province in a sweep on Tuesday and Wedneday and vowed to enforce Islamic Sharia law there.
The militia seized Jalalabad hours after government troops took control from a previously neutral council.
Later the militia fighters advanced on the 75-km (45-mile) eastern highway to Pakistan.
An Afghan government spokesman accused Pakistan on Wednesday of conspiring and aiding the Taleban attack, signalling a return to frosty relations between the two governments.

A Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman rejected the charge as unfounded and said Islamabad had been trying to promote intra-Afghan talks to bring peace to the war-shattered country. Pakistan evacuated eight staff members of its consulate in Jalalabad after government troops arrived there earlier on Wednesday to try to stop the pre-announced Taleban advance, a staff member said.
Taleban movement leader Mullah Mohammad Omar, based in the southern Afghan city of Kandahar, directed his field commanders to treat Nangar people well and harm no one, Taleban militia sources said.
Mullah Mohammad Rabbani was named the new Nangarhar governor replacing the previous neutral governor Haji Qadeer, who had fled to Pakistan on Tuesday.
